extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (calculus / real analysis) and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter giving precise criteria, theorems, and standard examples for limits of functions, one-sided limits, continuity (ε–δ and sequential), algebra of continuous functions, and the extreme/intermediate value theorems, with proofs and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order preservation of limits (Corollary 3.1.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are functions on S and c is a cluster point of S, suppose lim_{x→c} f(x) and lim_{x→c} g(x) both exist, and f(x) ≤ g(x) for all x ∈ S\{c}. Then lim_{x→c} f(x) ≤ lim_{x→c} g(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via taking any sequence x_n → c in S and applying the sequential lemma (Lemma 3.1.7). Use this to compare limits by comparing sequence values pointwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounds pass to limits (Corollary 3.1.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:S→R has a limit as x→c and there exist real numbers a and b with a ≤ f(x) ≤ b for all x near c (x∈S\{c}), then a ≤ lim_{x→c} f(x) ≤ b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the order preservation corollary using constant functions as bounds; the corollary follows from the sequential characterization of limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Squeeze (sandwich) theorem (Corollary 3.1.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f, g, h:S→R and for x near c we have f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ h(x), and if lim_{x→c} f(x) and lim_{x→c} h(x) exist and are equal, then lim_{x→c} g(x) exists and equals that common limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by applying the sequential lemma to sequences x_n→c and using f(x_n) ≤ g(x_n) ≤ h(x_n). Useful to show limits of complicated functions by comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra of limits (Corollary 3.1.12 / 3.1.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g have limits at c, then limits distribute over addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication, and multiplication: lim(f+g)=lim f + lim g, lim(f−g)=lim f − lim g, lim(αf)=α lim f, lim(fg)=lim f · lim g. If lim g ≠ 0 and g(x) ≠ 0 for x near c, then lim(f/g)=lim f / lim g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard limit laws; conditions for quotient explicitly require the denominator's limit to be nonzero and g to be nonzero near c. Proofs use sequence limits and basic algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential characterization of function limits (Lemma 3.1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f has limit L as x→c (c a cluster point) iff for every sequence (x_n) in S\{c} with x_n→c we have f(x_n)→L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma is used repeatedly to convert function-limit statements into statements about sequences; many proofs of corollaries and propositions rely on applying this sequential criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locality of limits / limits of restrictions (Definition 3.1.14 & Proposition 3.1.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: The limit of f at c depends only on values of f arbitrarily near c: if A⊂S contains a punctured neighborhood of c (i.e. there exists α>0 with (S∩(c−α,c+α))\{c} ⊂ A), then c is a cluster point of A iff of S; and lim_{x→c} f(x) (on S) = L iff lim_{x→c, x∈A} f(x) = L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis on A is necessary; for arbitrary restriction one only gets one-direction implications. Use this to work on smaller domains (tails, punctured neighborhoods) when checking limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-sided limits (Definition 3.1.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define right-hand and left-hand limits as limits of the restriction of f to S∩(c,∞) and S∩(−∞,c) respectively: lim_{x→c+} f(x) and lim_{x→c−} f(x) when c is a cluster point of those restricted sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-sided limits are limits of restrictions; Proposition 3.1.15 does not always apply. A function may have one-sided limits but no two-sided limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-sided limit iff equal one-sided limits (Proposition 3.1.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let c be a cluster point of both S∩(−∞,c) and S∩(c,∞). Then lim_{x→c} f(x) exists and equals L iff lim_{x→c−} f(x) = lim_{x→c+} f(x) = L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this equivalence to test for existence of two-sided limits by checking one-sided limits and equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon–delta definition of continuity (Definition 3.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:S→R and c∈S, f is continuous at c if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that whenever x∈S and |x−c|<δ we have |f(x)−f(c)|<ε. f is continuous on S if it is continuous at every c∈S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: δ may depend on both ε and c; this is the foundational (Weierstrass) definition used for rigorous continuity proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity ⇔ limit equals value (Proposition 3.2.2 (ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: If c is a cluster point of S then f is continuous at c iff lim_{x→c} f(x) exists and equals f(c). If c is not a cluster point, f is automatically continuous at c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This connects ε–δ continuity with limit-based continuity and is often used to switch viewpoints when proving continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential criterion for continuity (Proposition 3.2.2 (iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: f is continuous at c iff for every sequence (x_n) in S with x_n→c we have f(x_n)→f(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful and frequently used: to prove continuity show sequence images converge appropriately; to show discontinuity exhibit a sequence x_n→c whose images fail to converge to f(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity preserved under algebraic operations (Proposition 3.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are continuous at c then linear combinations, products, and quotients (provided denominator nonzero near c) are continuous at c. Concretely: if h(x)=f(x)+g(x), h(x)=f(x)g(x), or h(x)=f(x)/g(x) (with g(x)≠0 near c), then h is continuous at c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Corollary 3.1.12 (limit laws) or sequential arguments to prove these closure properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition preserves continuity (Proposition 3.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If g is continuous at c and f is continuous at g(c), then the composition f∘g is continuous at c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard proof via sequences: if x_n→c then g(x_n)→g(c) and hence f(g(x_n))→f(g(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuity detection via sequences (Proposition 3.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists a sequence x_n in S with x_n→c but f(x_n) does not converge to f(c) (either diverges or converges to a different value), then f is discontinuous at c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the contrapositive of the sequential continuity criterion and is used to produce counterexamples demonstrating discontinuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and canonical examples of discontinuities
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples and classifications: removable discontinuity when lim_{x→c} f(x) exists but f(c) differs (e.g., g with g(0)=1 but 0 elsewhere); jump discontinuity when left and right limits differ; functions discontinuous everywhere (Dirichlet function: 1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals); functions continuous at irrationals but discontinuous at rationals (Thomae 'popcorn' function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate phenomena to watch for when applying the sequential and ε–δ criteria; Thomae's function shows how rational-denominator bounds yield continuity at irrationals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomials are continuous (Proposition 3.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any polynomial f(x)=a_d x^d + ... + a_1 x + a_0 is continuous on R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by taking sequences and using algebraic closure of limits or by repeated application of continuity of x↦x and closure under algebraic operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous functions on closed bounded intervals are bounded (Lemma 3.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on the closed, bounded interval [a,b], then f([a,b]) is a bounded subset of R (there exists B such that |f(x)|≤B for all x∈[a,b]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contrapositive: if not bounded, construct sequence with unbounded images, extract convergent subsequence by Bolzano–Weierstrass, then continuity yields contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme Value Theorem (Minimum–Maximum theorem, Theorem 3.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on a closed, bounded interval [a,b], then f attains its absolute minimum and absolute maximum on [a,b]; i.e., there exist points c,d in [a,b] such that f(c)=sup_{[a,b]} f and f(d)=inf_{[a,b]} f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use boundedness of f, take sequences approaching sup/inf, extract convergent subsequences (Bolzano–Weierstrass), and pass limits through f to find points achieving extremal values. Domain being closed and bounded is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate Value Theorem / Bolzano (Theorem 3.3.8 & Lemma 3.3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on [a,b] and y is any number between f(a) and f(b), then there exists c∈(a,b) with f(c)=y. Lemma 3.3.7 provides the root-existence version: if f(a)<0<f(b) (or vice versa) then there exists c with f(c)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via bisection: construct nested intervals where sign changes, show endpoints converge to c and continuity yields f(c)=y. This theorem guarantees that continuous functions take all intermediate values on intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bisection method (constructive root-finding, Example 3.3.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithm obtained from the intermediate-value proof: given a continuous function with opposite signs at endpoints, repeatedly bisect the interval and select subinterval where sign change occurs to produce a sequence of nested intervals whose endpoints converge to a root.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a practical method for approximating roots; error shrinks by factor 1/2 each step. The textbook illustrates iterative numerical application to a polynomial to obtain successive approximations.
